verdicts.reasoning:
metering.py:1070 sets overrun = known > expected, with no threshold and for every purpose. metering.py:1151-1156 then sets the cycle to 'stopped', whatever the purpose, including workshop (listed in OUTSIDE_CYCLE_CAP :107). The next reserve() is refused by _cycle_refusal (:810-811) with category 'request'. The act loop turns that category into EndCycle('stopped') (loop.py:1161-1166), so the reflection is never attempted.

Live, cycle #46: #444 cost $0.3466 against $0.3441, the cycle stopped at 15:04:20, and #445 was refused 'wake cycle #46 is stopped' (0.13.0 report lines 604-605, events at 3447-3449). Message #63 in the same cycle had promised 'will propose it as a Printify product this cycle' (tool row 542). Of the 5 cycles since 0.12.0 (#42-#46), #44 and #46 were stopped by overruns.

My script replays #444's usage as a workshop call 2.94% over its quote. It prints 'overrun=True', "cycle: ('stopped', 'a call cost more than its worst-case estimate')" and "reflection refused: 'wake cycle #1 is stopped' category=request". Medium is fair: the stop is a documented design choice (DOCS.md:1539-1541), but the cost is real and frequent (2 of 6 workshop runs overran), and the stop gives no protection for an outside-cap purpose whose money is already spent.

verdicts.correction: 'Ended without a reflection or a journal' is too strong. Ember's code writes a system journal on every cycle end (loop.py:329-331). #44 and #46 have one: 'Cycle ended stopped: refused: wake cycle #N is stopped | Written by Ember's code: the reflection wrote no journal' (0.13.0 report lines 1367, 1369). What is lost is the agent's own reflection: its journal, lessons and handoff.

verdicts.reasoning:
Burn.cycle_cap (burn.py:53-54) and the event reserve (metering.py:452-457) change only cycles.cap_micros. rooms() gives a workshop the run cap (:677-678), and a review or study the daily cap (:679-680). Its money room (:684) subtracts neither the event reserve nor anything from the burn mode. No other code reads the burn mode for these purposes: the grep matches the finding, and the only maintenance-specific code is the sleep length at service.py:677-679. agenda.py:19 promises 'a scheduled cycle can't spend it', and that is false for workshop, review and study calls.

My script builds a scheduled cycle at 12:00 local time with $5 of a $7 day spent. It prints 'event reserve $1.4000', 'scheduled cycle cap $0.6000', 'rooms(workshop): ... may spend $1.5000' and 'rooms(review): ... may spend $2.0000'. A $1.45 workshop run is then admitted without an overrun, leaving $0.55 of the day. Forcing maintenance, it prints 'maintenance cycle cap $0.4000', 'rooms(workshop): may spend $1.5000' and 'rooms(review): may spend $7.0000'. The STATUS text 'This cycle may spend up to $1.00' comes from context.py:383 (0.13.0 report line 414).
verdicts.reproduction: scratchpad/verify-economy-0/v3_reserve.py. Part (a): reserve $1.40, scheduled cycle cap $0.60, workshop room $1.50, review/study room $2.00; a $1.45 run is admitted and the day reaches $6.45. Part (b), with burn._raw forced to maintenance: cycle cap $0.40, workshop room $1.50, review room $7.00.
verdicts.correction: (1) The workshop tool is limited to 2 runs per cycle (tools.py:766, per_cycle=2), and to 6 a day across cycles. So one maintenance or scheduled cycle can add at most 2 runs (up to about $3.00 at the owner's $1.50 run cap, plus overruns), not 6. (2) Cycle #44's $2.0045 against its $1.00 cap was an owner-triggered cycle (the workshop sits outside the cycle cap by design, DOCS.md:368-370). It shows the misleading STATUS line, not a live reserve or maintenance bypass: neither has happened live yet. (3) An event wake needs only an opening's cost (service.py:355-356; $0.06 on Sonnet, about $0.15 on Opus). In my run, one $1.45 workshop run still left enough to wake. Starving event wakes takes a second run in the same cycle or an overrun, both reachable. (4) The review's real bypass is small (its worst case is about $0.15); the workshop is what matters.

OUTSIDE_CYCLE_CAP includes CONSOLIDATE and CRITIC (metering.py:107), and _money_refusal skips the cycle-cap check for them (:845). But Books.cycle_spend(outside_cap=False) hard-codes "purpose NOT IN ('workshop', 'review', 'study')" (ledger.py:397), so critic and consolidation costs are subtracted from every later call's cycle room. rooms() also gives them the cycle room as their own cap (else branch, metering.py:681-682). verdicts.label: reproduced
verdicts.reasoning:
Loop._affordable (loop.py:1267-1273) calls quote(request), expected(request), quote(reflect), prompt_tokens(request) and expected(reflect). expected() calls quote() and then _plan() again (metering.py:547-551), and every _plan calls transport.count_tokens (:587-591), so that is 7 counts. reserve() adds an 8th (:701-705). AnthropicTransport.count_tokens is an HTTP request with max_retries=2 and a 30 s timeout. It falls back to rough_token_count (bytes/2 + 600, about twice the real count for English) (anthropic_transport.py:153-158).

I ran a full scripted wake cycle through Agent.run_cycle with a transport that logs calls. It showed 1 count before the plan, 8 before each of the 3 work steps, and 3 before the reflection. The one live count failure was an InternalServerError at 2026-09-29T14:17:37. It is a latency and robustness cost, not money: low.
